messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rafael had been a bus driver for over a decade, ferrying passengers across the city with ease. But it was on one fateful evening, three years ago, that his life took a drastic turn. As he drove through a crowded intersection, police sirens blared behind him. Rafael pulled over, expecting a routine traffic stop. Instead, officers stormed onto the bus, shouting and waving their guns. Rafael's memories of what happened next were hazy, but one moment stuck with him: an officer's aggressive tone as he demanded Rafael step off the bus. The incident sparked a flurry of news reports about police brutality, leaving Rafael feeling shaken and helpless. In the months that followed, Rafael started experiencing sudden, vivid recollections of that night – Intrusive Memories that would surface without warning, transporting him back to the midst of chaos. When talking about the event with friends or family, he'd relive the anxiety, his heart racing as if it were happening all over again. Even the sight of police officers on the street made him anxious; Authority Presence seemed to trigger an automatic response within him. To cope, Rafael began hiding behind Face Hiding – literally covering his face with his hands when memories flooded back or when confronted with triggers in his daily routine. He started avoiding social gatherings and parties, opting instead for solitary activities like watching TV or listening to loud music as a Sensory Distraction. As the Intrusive Memories persisted, Rafael's irritability grew; he'd snap at passengers on the bus, and even found himself involved in heated arguments with fellow drivers during break times. His Concentration suffered too – he struggled to focus on the road ahead, his mind constantly wandering back to that fateful evening. He started checking doors and windows obsessively before leaving for work each morning, Door and Lock Checking becoming a new ritual. For Rafael, it felt like the world had indeed become a more treacherous place since the incident – World is Dangerous was no longer just an abstract concept but a daily reality he faced head-on. He also began to sense that his connection with the community around him had frayed; Lost Community seemed to echo in every interaction he now found strained or forced. And then there was Mistrust, creeping into even the most mundane relationships – passengers who got on at the wrong stop, fellow drivers who honked too loudly... People can't be trusted. This perpetual wariness bled into his relationships outside of work as well. As Rafael navigated this web of emotions and reactions, he couldn't shake off the feeling that every new trigger only further convinced him that the world was an unforgiving place – each threat fuelling more Negative Appraisals about himself and others. At times, these very fears led him to inadvertently stumble upon triggers – like accidentally watching a news clip about police brutality or bumping into an officer on his route – perpetuating a cycle of anxiety he felt powerless to break. Rafael's life as a bus driver had become a minefield; the more he struggled to cope with Intrusive Memories and Threat, the more Maladaptive Strategies he employed. Avoid People became his default response, leaving him isolated from friends and family. Sensory Distraction provided fleeting respite but left him fatigued and emotionally drained. And yet, every time Rafael managed to momentarily escape this labyrinth of anxiety, a new trigger would emerge – another Intrusive Memory, an unexpected run-in with an officer – sending him tumbling back into the abyss. When he finally mustered the courage to seek help, Rafael's world had shrunk dramatically; his fears and mistrust now dominated every interaction. He knew that seeking therapy wouldn't magically erase the trauma or restore trust overnight, but perhaps it could teach him new ways to navigate this treacherous landscape – maybe even show him a path back towards connection and community. (Note: I made some minor adjustments in wording and sentence structure for better flow while keeping the original requirements intact)
